diff-soup: GPU-native Differentiable Simulation and Inference for Large-scale Stiff Dynamical Systems

Samuel Degnan-Morgenstern<sup>a</sup>, Martin Z. Bazant<sup>a,b,∗</sup>

<sup>_a_</sup>_Department of Chemical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25 Ames St., Cambridge, MA 02139, USA_

<sup>_b_</sup>_Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 182 Memorial Dr., Cambridge, MA 02139, USA_

**Abstract**

Learning physical models from spatiotemporal data requires simulating systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) and differentiating through their solution. Upon spatial discretization, these models give rise to stiff dynamical systems that require repeatedly solving large, sparse linear systems. Traditional scientific computing frameworks are largely CPU-based and require problem-specific tuning to accelerate, scale, and differentiate. In this work, we introduce diff-soup, a differentiable, sparse-oriented, unified PDE suite for GPU-native simulation and inference of large, stiff dynamical systems. Built in JAX, diff-soup provides 1) a fully differentiable design for problems with sparse structure, 2) scaling to large problems through the NVIDIA cuDSS sparse direct solver with model and data multi-GPU parallelism, and 3) end-to-end PDE-constrained optimization, from classical statistical inference to embedded deep learning. On stiff PDE benchmarks, diff-soup outperforms established CPU- and GPU-based frameworks by one to two orders of magnitude in both forward solves and gradients. We demonstrate both a classical Bayesian inference workflow, identifying constitutive relationships, and a modern deep learning workflow, training a neural field for the catalyst activity of a three-dimensional packed bed reactor. We provide diff-soup as an open-source repository to facilitate research in computational science and engineering.

_Nature of problem:_ Computational modeling of time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) gives rise to large systems of stiff ordinary differential equations and differential-algebraic equations. Robust and efficient integration of these systems requires implicit variable step, variable order (VSVO) methods such as BDF and NDF, whose predominant cost is the repeated factorization and solution of large sparse linear systems. The established stiff integration libraries run these operations on the CPU, and the general-purpose implicit ODE/DAE time- integration libraries of the `JAX` ecosystem rely on dense linear algebra, so large two- and three-dimensional problems remain out of reach for GPU-native, differentiable simulation. These challenges have limited the adoption of machine learning in general multiphysics modeling workflows.

_Solution method:_ We introduce diff-soup, a general-purpose differentiable, sparse- oriented unified PDE suite for GPU-accelerated multiphysics modeling, simulation, and inference. We provide a user-friendly Recipe API that models complex physical systems in math-like notation on both structured and unstructured domains with the finite difference, finite volume, and finite element methods. For fast simulation, we implement sparse Jacobian assembly by automatic differentiation with graph coloring, three VSVO stiff integrators written natively in `JAX`, and a wrapper to the NVIDIA `cuDSS` sparse direct linear solver on the GPU. All simulations are fully differentiable to second order, enabling large-scale PDE-constrained optimization. Using these derivatives, we provide an inference module for PDE-constrained least- squares problems, from classical frequentist and Bayesian inference to modern deep learning approaches. Both simulation and inference exploit batched solves, data parallelism, and model parallelism to scale to large problems.

_Additional comments including restrictions and unusual features:_ This article describes `diff-soup` 1.0.0. The package runs on Linux x86\_64 with Python 3.12 and `JAX` 0.11. GPU execution requires an NVIDIA GPU with a CUDA 12 or CUDA 13 driver and `cuDSS` 1.0 or newer, which is installed from NVIDIA’s Python wheels.

Without a GPU, every solver runs on the CPU through the KLU and dense backends. Differential-algebraic equations are supported up to index one. Solves can be distributed across several GPUs and across the nodes of a cluster.

_Keywords:_ Partial differential equations, Differentiable simulation, PDE-constrained optimization, GPU sparse direct linear solver, Stiff dynamical systems

## 1. Introduction

The numerical simulation of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) is fundamental to science and engineering, providing quantitative predictions of coupled transport, reaction, and thermodynamic processes across multiple length and time scales. Important examples include numerical weather and climate prediction [1, 2], turbulent and reacting flows [3, 4], microstructure evolution in materials [5, 6, 7], electrochemical energy storage [8, 9, 10], and biological pattern formation [11, 12]. Recent advances are bridging these physical models with data-driven methods to enable the learning, design, and control of physical systems directly from data [13, 14, 15]. In weather and climate modeling, learned components are now embedded within physical solvers [16, 17], and in fluid mechanics, neural networks are trained through differentiable solvers to correct and accelerate simulations [18, 19, 20]. Governing equations and constitutive relationships have been inferred directly from spatiotemporal data [21, 22, 23], and PDE-constrained optimization has been extended from inference to control [24, 25]. At the same time, high-resolution imaging techniques such as _operando_ microscopy are making spatially resolved data increasingly available for high-dimensional PDE models [26, 27, 28]. Exploiting such datasets requires software that can simulate these models at the scale of the experiment and differentiate through the simulation.

Both requirements are difficult to meet for PDEs, because once discretized in space, they fall into the important class of stiff dynamical systems [29]. Stiff problems exhibit multiple competing time scales, such that the slowly varying solution of interest is surrounded by rapidly varying nearby solutions that force a numerical integrator to take small time steps [30]. The integration of stiff systems is a well-established field of computational science, with libraries such as SUNDIALS [31, 32], PETSc [33], `DifferentialEquations.jl` [34], and the MATLAB ODE suite [35]<tbc>

<tbc>providing specialized implicit integrators. To both solve and take gradients, these methods require Jacobians which are either manually derived or computed through potentially-inaccurate finite-difference rules, expensive dense automatic differentiation, or performant sparse automatic differentiation. Gradients additionally require complex, bespoke rules for parameter sensitivities that do not easily compose with stiff solvers.

A central component of these algorithms is the repeated solution of large linear systems. For PDEs, the local structure of the differential operators gives rise to a discrete sparse representation, which is exploited either by sparse direct solvers, such as KLU [36], SuperLU [37], and UMFPACK [38], or by iterative Newton-Krylov methods like GMRES [39, 40]. Sparse direct solvers are robust across a wide range of problems but have traditionally been run on the CPU, with GPU-accelerated factorizations emerging only recently [41, 42]. Newton-Krylov methods, in contrast, require only Jacobian-vector products and are naturally implemented on GPUs, but their fast and stable convergence depends on a problem-specific preconditioner.

Existing GPU efforts fall into three groups: hybrid codes that keep the integrator on the CPU and offload Krylov kernels, batched solvers for many small systems, and JAX frameworks that target specific physics or rely on dense linear algebra. SUNDIALS and PETSc support hybrid execution, in which the time integrator remains on the host while large systems are solved with Newton-Krylov methods on the GPU [43, 44]. `DiffEqGPU.jl` [45] and `jaxdae` [46] efficiently batch many small problems on the GPU. Differentiable PDE solvers such as `JAX-CFD` [20], `JAX-Fluids` [47], and `JAX-FEM` [48] compose GPU-accelerated simulation with machine learning for specific physics or discretizations, while the general-purpose implicit integrators of `diffrax` [49] rely on dense linear algebra by default. What remains missing is robust GPU parallelism within a single large, stiff solve, as needed for two- and three- dimensional PDEs, without relying on a problem-specific preconditioner. To our knowledge, no existing package in the Python/JAX ecosystem natively composes GPU sparse direct solvers, variable step, variable order (VSVO) time integration, and sparse automatic differentiation for the differentiable simulation of large dynamical systems.

The recent release of `cuDSS` by NVIDIA [50], a sparse direct solver that performs the numerical factorization and the triangular solves on the GPU, removes the major bottleneck in the robust integration of large-scale PDEs. In this work, we present `diff-soup`, a GPU-native package for the simulation and inference of large, stiff PDE systems, built around the `cuDSS`<tbc>

linear solver and sparse automatic differentiation in `JAX`. Traditionally, differential equation software has been developed for small model problems and extended to large multiphysics systems afterwards, whereas we take the opposite approach and design every component around the sparse structure of large discretized PDEs. `diff-soup` provides the standard numerical tools of a large-scale stiff solver, including VSVO integrators for stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and index-1 differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) with consistent initialization, event handling, and sparse automatic differentiation, together with finite difference, finite volume, and finite element discretizations on grids and meshes. Beyond these standard tools, `diff-soup` is distinguished from existing stiff solvers by

1. a GPU-native and fully differentiable design that is specialized to problems with sparse structure,<tbc>

2. accelerator-specific techniques for reaching large problems, namely reduced precision, batched solves, and multi-GPU parallelism, and<tbc>

3. end-to-end workflows for PDE-constrained optimization, with second- order optimizers, multiple shooting, and statistical inference, that compose with `JAX` libraries such as `equinox` [51], `optax` [52], and `blackjax` [53] for embedded deep learning models and uncertainty quantification.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the computational background on VSVO time integration, sparse methods, and differentiable simulation. Section 3 describes the modeling, simulation, and inference modules of `diff-soup`. In Section 4, we benchmark forward solves and gradients against SUNDIALS, PETSc, `DifferentialEquations.jl`, MATLAB, and `diffrax`, and we examine reduced precision and multi-GPU execution. In Section 5, we demonstrate two end-to-end applications, the Bayesian inference of the constitutive relationships of a phase-separating material from image data and the training of a neural field embedded in a three-dimensional packed bed reactor model.

## 2. Mathematical Background

In this work, we consider time-dependent systems that take the general form of a differential-algebraic equation

\(0=F(y,y',\theta,z(t),t),\) (1)

where \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the state, _t_ is time, \(\theta\) is the parameter vector, and _z(t_) is the control state that carries externally prescribed inputs. These systems are solved on the interval [_t_<sub>0</sub>_,t<sub>f</sub>_] and the initial state is prescribed as _y(t=t_<sub>0</sub>)=_y_<sub>0</sub>. For many systems, this generally reduces to mass-matrix form

\(M(y,t)\cdot y'=f(y,\theta,z(t),t),\) (2)

where _M(y,t_) is the (non-)singular mass matrix. We partition the state variable into the local differential states, \(y_d\in\mathbb{R}^{n_d}\), which carry explicit time derivatives in the governing form, local algebraic states, \(y_a\in\mathbb{R}^{n_a}\), which are specified through algebraic constraints with a sparse structure, and global algebraic variables, \(y_g\in\mathbb{R}^{n_g}\), _n<sub>g</sub>_, which are treated as dense and typically arise from global constraints on the state variables. Since \(n_g\checkmark n_a+n_d\), this split lets us handle the global variables separately (Sec. 2.2). In this section, we discuss the relevant background on the three main computational aspects of `diff-soup`: robust methods for numerical integration of stiff equations, exploiting sparse structure to accelerate computations, and computing sensitivities of differential algebraic equations for PDE-constrained optimization.

## 2.1. Variable Step, Variable Order Algorithms

In this work, we consider stiff systems with a defined sparse structure, as is typical for the discretization of partial differential equations using the method of lines. Partial differential equations are naturally stiff due to the decaying spectrum of the underlying differential operators that translates to a large, resolution-dependent ratio between the minimum and maximum eigenvalues [29]. Stable integration therefore requires specialized methods, since explicit methods are limited by a CFL time scale and naive implicit methods need a prohibitive number of steps to resolve fast dynamics.[54, 55]. We consider the variable step, variable order (VSVO) class of numerical integration algorithms [56, 57] which we separate into two families based on the discretization of the time derivative: backward differentiation formula (BDF) [58] in fixed-leading-coefficient (FLC) form [59] and the numerical differentiation formula (NDF) [60] in quasi-constant step size (QSS) form [35]. We implement three algorithms in `diff-soup`: the JAX implicit differential algebraic (`JIDA`) solver based on the popular `IDA` implementation in SUNDIALS [31], the JAX BDF solver (`JBDF`) based on the `CVODE\_BDF` implementation in SUNDIALS [31] and `FBDF` implementation in `DifferentialEquations.jl` [34], and the JAX NDF solver (`JNDF`) based on the `ode15s` algorithm [35] and implementation of `QNDF` in `DifferentialEquations.jl` [34].

For large systems, the dominant computational bottlenecks are the formation of _J<sub>n</sub>_ and the subsequent factorization of the pencil matrix _W<sub>n</sub>_ during the linear solve at each iteration of Eq. (4) \[29, 61\]. The modified Newton iteration freezes both quantities as long as possible, even though reusing the old Jacobian reduces the convergence rate of Newton’s method from quadratic to linear \[61\]. As such, the development of reliable heuristics for efficient reuse of _J_ across both nonlinear solver iterations and time steps has been an intense area of research and hinges on the interplay between caching rules and the step size and order controllers, which we describe in turn \[29, 31\].

For the caching rules, all three solvers guard the nonlinear iteration with a two-tier setup gate that re-evaluates the cached Jacobian only when it has aged past a step budget or when a convergence failure has occurred [31]. Otherwise, when the ratio of the current \(\gamma_n\) to the value frozen into the factors of _W<sub>n</sub>_ has drifted outside a deadband, the mass-matrix engines rebuild the pencil \(\frac{1}{\gamma_n}M-J_n\) from the saved _J<sub>n</sub>_ without re-differentiation [31]. `JIDA` extends the same reuse to the fully implicit form, recomposing _W<sub>n</sub>_ from the saved \(\partial F/\partial y\) while re-evaluating only \(\partial F/\partial y'\), whereas the reference DAE integrator refreshes both partial derivatives at every setup [63, 31]. A convergence-rate memory extrapolates the contraction of the iteration and declares divergence after two iterations rather than exhausting the iteration budget, and failed steps escalate through a ladder that refreshes the Jacobian and shrinks the step [35, 31]. This cost hierarchy shapes the control layer that follows, because any change of the step size or the order moves \(\gamma_n\) and invalidates the saved factors, so the controllers are built to change both quantities only as often as accuracy demands.

For the local error control, each solver estimates the local truncation error \(\widehat{e}_{n+1}\) of the converged step from the difference between the predictor and the corrected solution, scaled by an order-dependent constant, and measures it in the weighted root-mean-square (WRMS) norm

\(\text{err}=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(\frac{\widehat{e}_{n+1,i}}{w_i}\big)^2\right)^{1/2},w_i=\text{atol}+\text{rtol}|y_i|,\) (5)

where the weight _w<sub>i</sub>_ blends the absolute tolerance atol and the relative tolerance rtol so that \(\text{err}\le 1\) accepts the step as accurate to the requested tolerances [61, 31]. Because the stored history spans the adjacent orders, the same difference tables furnish companion error estimates at orders _q_-1 and _q_+1 at negligible additional cost, and these three estimates drive both the step size and the order selection [56, 29].

Each controller converts the error estimate at order _q_ into a proposed growth factor for the step size, \(\eta=h_{n+1}/h_n\), through a safety-biased power law of the form \(\eta\propto\text{err}^{-1/(q+1)}\), and passes the proposal through a deadband around unity that holds the step size, and thereby the saved factors of _W<sub>n</sub>_, unless the predicted change is large enough to justify a refactorization [61]. The companion estimates at the adjacent orders enter the same way, each candidate order competing through its own estimate. Beneath the controllers, the QSS NDF and FLC BDF families differ in the response of the multistep coefficients in Eq. (3) to a realized change in the step-size history. The QSS implementation retains the constant-step coefficients at every step, which makes the formula and its error estimates exact only on a uniform step grid, so it prefers long runs at a fixed step size, defers order changes until the history has run uniformly for several steps, and answers a realized change by rescaling the entire backward-difference history onto the new grid [35]. The fully variable-coefficient alternative of EPISODE and VODE recomputes every coefficient from the realized nonuniform history, which gives the strongest stability on rapidly varying steps but lets every change in the history perturb the iteration matrix, sacrificing the reuse of the factorization [57, 64]. ## 2.2. Exploiting Sparsity

As established above, the two dominant computational bottlenecks of the VSVO integration are the formation of the Jacobian _J<sub>n</sub>_ and the factorization of the pencil matrix _W<sub>n</sub>_ within the modified Newton iteration [29, 61]. Conventional discretization methods for PDEs, such as the finite difference method (FDM), the finite volume method (FVM), and the finite element method (FEM), represent local differential operators in a sparse form such that each component of _y_ couples to a bounded set of neighbors, so the Jacobian \(J_n=\partial f/\partial y\) has _O(n_) nonzero entries in a pattern that is fixed by the discretization _a priori_. Exploiting this property, we store _J<sub>n</sub>_ and _W<sub>n</sub>_ in sparse data structures that drastically reduce the memory footprint. In this section, we describe how `diff-soup` uses this structure to speed up the Jacobian computation, pencil matrix factorization, and efficiently handle dense, global variables.

Traditionally, differential equation libraries offer three routes to the Jacobian: analytical Jacobians supplied by hand, as in SUNDIALS and PETSc<tbc>

<tbc>[31, 66], which is cumbersome and error-prone for all but the simplest right- hand sides; finite difference approximations, whose truncation and round-off errors degrade the convergence of the Newton iteration [31]; and dense automatic differentiation, which is exact but requires _n_ tangent or cotangent evaluations therefore scaling as _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) [67]. More recently, sparse automatic differentiation has matured in the Julia ecosystem, which pairs automatic sparsity detection with graph coloring to compress the Jacobian into a small number of directional derivatives and deploys the approach throughout its differential equation solvers [34, 68].

`diff-soup` builds on this template with the automatic differentiation machinery of `JAX` [69]. We assemble the pattern symbolically by composing the declared patterns of the operators that constitute the right-hand side and we compress the Jacobian following the Curtis-Powell-Reid (CPR) approach with a greedy, largest-first coloring of its column intersection graph [70, 71, 72]. The colors define a seed matrix \(V\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n_c}\), whose _k_-th column sums the unit vectors of the columns assigned to color _k_, and every nonzero entry of _J_ can be read off from the compressed product

\(B=JV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n_c},\) (6)

because structurally orthogonal columns deposit their entries into disjoint rows of _B_. For the bounded stencils of FDM and FVM discretizations, _n<sub>c</sub>_ is set by the stencil width independent of the resolution, so \(n_c\checkmark n\), and we compute all _n<sub>c</sub>_ tangent propagations in parallel with the `jax.vmap` operator, reducing the cost of the Jacobian from _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) to _O(n_). The same batching applies to FEM kernels, where `jax.vmap` evaluates the element-local residuals across all elements, and the local kernels are differentiated and scattered to assemble the sparse Jacobian in _O(n_).

Because the global variables couple broadly to the state, they typically produce dense rows and columns that give _J_ an arrowhead structure. Bidirectional coloring methods can compress such patterns by combining forward and reverse passes [71, 72], but under the unidirectional column coloring we employ, a single dense row makes every pair of columns share a row, so each column needs its own color. We therefore exclude the global variables and equations from the sparsity pattern and compute the two dense coupling blocks with local kernels: the _n<sub>g</sub>_ dense rows \(\partial f_g/\partial y\) are evaluated in reverse mode with one `jax.jacrev` cotangent per global equation, and the _n<sub>g</sub>_ dense columns \(\partial f/\partial y_g\) in forward mode with one `jax.jacfwd` tangent per global variable.

Using this approach, for most PDE problems the remaining computational bottleneck is the factorization of the pencil matrix _W<sub>n</sub>_ during the linear solve of Eq. (4). Among the classical factorizations, we consider only the LU decomposition, as the pencil matrix _W<sub>n</sub>_ is nonsymmetric for general right-hand sides, which precludes the Cholesky factorization, while the QR factorization roughly doubles the operation count and produces denser factors, which reserves it for ill-conditioned least-squares problems [73]. An LU solver proceeds in three phases: an analysis phase that determines the pivoting strategy and the structure of the factors, a factorization phase that computes the lower and upper triangular factors _L_ and _U_, and a solve phase that applies them through forward and backward substitution [55]. For a dense matrix, the LU factorization costs _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) while each subsequent solve costs only _O(n_<sup>2</sup>), so the algorithm concentrates the expense in the analysis and factorization to make the solves fast. This front-loaded cost profile is well matched to the VSVO structure, because the setup gate freezes the pencil across Newton iterations and time steps, so a single factorization is reused for many cheap triangular solves [61, 31]. Nevertheless, the cubic cost of factorization is an immense barrier for large systems. Much research has focused on linear solvers that exploit sparsity to reduce this cubic cost, and for the purpose of our discussion, we limit ourselves to two families: iterative Newton-Krylov methods and sparse direct solvers [74, 73].

Newton-Krylov methods solve the linearized system in a reduced Krylov subspace \(\mathcal{K}_m=\mathrm{span}\{v,W_nv,W_n^2v,\dots,W_n^{m-1}v\}\) and therefore require only matrix-vector products with _W<sub>n</sub>_, and hence only Jacobian-vector products, which makes them attractive for large systems [40]. The workhorse algorithm implemented in most libraries is the generalized minimal residual (GMRES) method, which builds an orthonormal basis of K_<sub>m</sub>_ and selects the iterate that minimizes the residual norm over the subspace, imposing no symmetry requirements on _W_ [39]. However, the convergence of the Krylov iteration deteriorates on the ill-conditioned spectra that stiff discretizations produce, and much work has been devoted to preconditioners that transform the system before the iteration [74]. The best preconditioners are often problem specific, since their goal is to cluster the eigenvalues of the preconditioned system near unity, and the two most common generic choices are the incomplete LU (ILU) factorization and algebraic multigrid (AMG), for which we refer the reader to Saad [74] and Ruge and Stüben [75] for further details.

In contrast to the iterative methods, sparse direct solvers operate on the sparse representation of _W_ itself and require no problem-specific tuning.<tbc>

Sparse analogs of the LU factorization, such as the KLU algorithm, retain the analysis, factorization, and solve structure while confining the computation to the nonzero matrix entries \[36\]. In general, the factors of a sparse matrix are generally much denser than the matrix itself due to fill in during elimination, so the analysis phase must compute a fill-reducing ordering and pay careful attention to the interaction between ordering, pivoting, and sparsity \[73\]. For matrices arising from two- and three-dimensional meshes under nested dissection orderings, the factorization costs _O(n_<sup>3/2</sup>) and _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) respectively in the total number of unknowns _n_, a substantial reduction from the dense _O(n_<sup>3</sup>) although still superlinear \[76, 73\]. Sparse elimination is inherently serial and branching heavy, so these methods have traditionally struggled to exploit CPU and GPU parallelism. `SuperLU\_MT` achieved a CPU-parallel factorization by scheduling the independent subtrees of the elimination tree across threads and pipelining the remaining panel updates, and we refer the reader to Demmel et al. \[77\] for the details of the algorithm. Practical GPU implementations have emerged only recently, most notably NVIDIA’s cuDSS, a GPU-accelerated sparse direct solver. We have developed `diff-soup` around `cuDSS`, mapping its three phases onto the caching structure of the integrator: the symbolic analysis is performed once per sparsity pattern, which the discretization fixes _a priori_, the numeric factorization is repeated only when the setup gate refreshes _W<sub>n</sub>_, and the cached factors serve every Newton iterate in between through cheap triangular solves. This solver has also allowed us to explore GPU-specific strategies for accelerating the computation, such as working in reduced precision, batching independent solves in parallel, and employing multi-GPU execution, as we discuss in Section 4.

Differentiable Simulation and PDE-constrained Optimization Recent progress in scientific machine learning has concentrated on differentiable simulation for PDE-constrained applications in learning, inference, design, control, and uncertainty quantification [15, 78, 79, 24, 25]. The PDE- constrained optimization problem takes the form \(min_\theta\mathcal{L}\big(y(t,\theta),\theta\big),\)
\(\text{s.t.}M(y,t)\cdot y'=f(y,\theta,z(t),t),\) (9) where L is a scalar cost function and \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n_\theta}\) collects the parameters of interest. Conventional first-order optimization requires the total derivative of the cost with respect to the parameters, \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathcal{L}\big(y(t,\theta),\theta\big)=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta}+\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\theta},\) (10) where the central quantity is the sensitivity matrix \(\partial y/\partial\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n_\theta}\), the derivative of the solution with respect to the parameters. To compute the sensitivity matrix, one must differentiate Eq. (2) with respect to the parameters using either the continuous or discrete sensitivity paradigm. Optimize-then-discretize derives continuous auxiliary equations for the sensitivities and integrates them numerically alongside the state, as in the CVODES and IDAS integrators of SUNDIALS [80, 31] Discretize- then-optimize differentiates the discrete computational graph of the solver program and can be implemented in three ways: hand-derived discrete adjoints, as in PETSc’s `TSAjoint` [33, 81] and FATODE [82]; symbolic derivation of the adjoint from the recorded variational forms of a finite element

solve, as in `dolfin-adjoint` [83]; and automatic differentiation (AD) of the solver’s computational graph, as in `diffrax` and this work [49, 69]. The Julia ecosystem exposes both routes behind a common sensitivity interface [34, 15]. Both the continuous and discrete paradigms can be computed in forward mode, where one tangent per parameter is propagated forward, or reverse (adjoint) mode, where one cotangent per scalar cost traverses backwards. This gives four methods as described in detail in this section and compared in  2: forward sensitivity analysis (FSA) and adjoint sensitivity analysis (ASA) for continuous sensitivities [84, 31], and forward and reverse AD for discrete sensitivities, as implemented in `diff-soup` [49].

FSA differentiates the governing equations with respect to each parameter. For a state-independent mass matrix, differentiating Eq. (2) with respect to \(\theta_j\) yields the tangent system

\(Ms'_j=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}s_j+\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_j},\) (11)

where \(s_j=\partial y/\partial\theta_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the _j_-th column of the sensitivity matrix, and the fully implicit form of Eq. (1) differentiates the same way into \(\partial F/\partial ys_j+\partial F/\partial y's'_j+\partial F/\partial\theta_j=0\). The tangent systems are linear and share the pencil matrix _W_ with the forward solve, so the sensitivities advance alongside the state through cheap solves with the cached factors [31]. The sensitivity matrix is also useful beyond the gradient, as for least-squares cost functions the product \((\partial y/\partial\theta)^T(\partial y/\partial\theta)\) is the canonical Gauss-Newton approximation to the Hessian. Because the integrator carries one tangent system per parameter, the cost of FSA scales as \(O(n_\theta T(n))\), where _T(n_) denotes the cost of one forward VSVO solve under the sparse methods above.

Alternatively, forward-mode AD propagates tangents through the discrete computational graph of the adaptive integration loop, which `diff-soup` implements as a `lax.while` loop \[69\] as shown in Figure 2. The tangent \(\dot{y}_n=\frac{\partial y_n}{\partial\theta}\dot{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as the directional derivative of the accepted state along a seed direction \(\dot{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_\theta}\), and forward mode advances one tangent per<tbc>

<tbc>seed [67]. Unrolled, the loop is a chain of accepted steps, and each step is an implicit function of the parameters and of the _k_ stored history states, because the corrector equation _G<sub>n</sub>(y_<sub>_n_+1</sub>)=0 inherits the stored states through the multistep formula and the parameters through the right-hand side. Rather than naively differentiating through the Newton algorithm, we apply the implicit function theorem at the converged root [49, 85], which turns the constant mass matrix step dependence into the tangent recurrence

\(W_n\dot{y}_{n+1}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\dot{\theta}-\frac{1}{\gamma_n}M\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j\dot{y}_{n+1-j},\) (12)

where _W<sub>n</sub>_ is the exact pencil of Eq. (4) evaluated at the root, the first term carries the direct parameter dependence, and the sum carries the stored history tangents into the new step. To ensure the correctness of the derivative, a fresh pencil matrix _W<sub>n</sub>_ and factorization must be used at an extra computational cost rather than the potentially stale factor used by the forward program. We employ the frozen-controller approximation, such that we apply gradient truncation to the adaptive order and step size control flow. Instead, tangents differentiate the realized control schedule as a fixed discretization [49]. Because forward mode AD carries one tangent per seed, the cost retains the \(O(n_\theta T(n))\) scaling of FSA. To reduce practical cost, we leverage the shared pencil factorization to efficiently batch the tangent computation at each step.

For systems with many parameters, such as training modern deep neural networks, the \(O(n_\theta T(n))\) scaling of the forward methods renders differentiation practically infeasible. Fortunately, reverse-mode and adjoint methods compute the gradient of a scalar cost directly, at a cost that no longer multiplies in \(n_\theta\). In the continuous setting, adjoint sensitivity analysis introduces the costate \(\lambda(t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and, for a constant mass matrix and a cost of integral form \(\mathcal{L}=\int_{t_0}^{t_f}g(y,\theta,t)dt\), integrates the adjoint system backward from _t<sub>f</sub>_,<tbc>

\(M^T\lambda'=-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}^T\lambda-\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}^T,\lambda(t_f)=0,\) (13)

<tbc>after which the gradient follows from the quadrature

\(\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\theta}=\int_{t_0}^{t_f}\big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial\theta}+\lambda^T\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\big)dt+\lambda(t_0)^TM\frac{\partial y_0}{\partial\theta},\) (14)

where _y_<sub>0</sub> carries any parameter dependence of the initial state and terminal costs enter through a nonzero terminal condition. For a singular mass matrix, the terminal condition must itself be consistently initialized, because the algebraic components of the costate are determined by the adjoint constraints, and we refer the reader to Cao et al. \[84\] for the derivation in the fully implicit and higher-index settings.

The backward solve of Eq. (13) requires the forward trajectory _y(t_), and the implementations trade memory against recomputation through three strategies: a dense interpolant of the forward solution, checkpointing with segment recomputation, and re-integration of the state backward in time alongside the adjoint \[78, 34\]. The Julia ecosystem pairs the interpolant with an adaptive Gauss quadrature of the gradient integral in Eq. (14), which typically converges in far fewer evaluations than the time integration itself \[34, 86\]. For stiff problems, however, two stability concerns constrain these choices: the backward re-integration of the state, popularized for neural ODEs \[87\], is unstable because the reversed dissipative dynamics amplify small forward errors, and the adjoint system inherits the stiffness of the forward problem, so it must itself be integrated implicitly with the same sparse linear algebra as the forward solve \[86\]. The number of costates is parameter independent and quadrature accumulates the \(n_\theta\) gradient components additively, so the total cost scales as \(O(T(n)+n_\theta)\).

In the JAX-native engines, we instead differentiate the adaptive control loop in reverse mode as a discrete adjoint using the checkpointed while loop in `equinox`, which implements the optimal online checkpointing algorithms of Stumm and Walther \[88\] and Wang et al. \[89\]. In reverse mode, the tangent solve of Eq. (12) transposes, and each step propagates the cotangent \(\bar{y}_{n+1}=\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dy_{n+1}}^T\) backward through one linear solve with \(W_n^T\), traversing the chain of Figure 2 from the cost to the parameters. Rather than storing the trajectory, the loop retains \(O(\sqrt{n_\text{steps}})\) checkpoints of the accepted states by default, where _n_steps is the user-prescribed step ceiling, and recomputes the segments between them during the backward sweep, bounding the memory at \(O(\sqrt{n_\text{steps}}n)\). One backward sweep costs a constant recomputation of the forward solve and accumulates the parameter cotangent \(\bar{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_\theta}\) additively across the steps, so the gradient scales as \(O(T(n)+n_\theta)\). As in forward mode AD, we employ the frozen-controller assumption, so cotangents flow only through the accepted steps, and we refer the reader to Kidger \[49\] and the `diffrax` documentation for a detailed treatment of these checkpointing and<tbc>

Beyond smooth trajectories, the control state _z(t_) introduces events, such as protocol switches and state-triggered conditions, that stop the integration, update the state, and restart it from a consistent state. Because the frozen- controller assumption fixes the time grid, the discrete computational graph alone would miss how the switch time moves with the parameters, so we attach custom JVP and VJP rules to each event. We implement three second- order compositions through the solver: forward-over-forward differentiation, which propagates second-order tangents along the realized trajectory and assembles the full \(n_\theta\times n_\theta\) Hessian at \(O(n_\theta^2T(n))\), reverse-over-forward differentiation, which computes gradients of scalar criteria built from the solution and its forward sensitivities through one reverse sweep over the tangent solve at \(O(n_\theta T(n))\), and forward-over-reverse differentiation, the canonical strategy for Hessian-vector products [67], which differentiates the checkpointed gradient in forward mode and delivers each product at a constant multiple of the gradient cost, \(O(T(n)+n_\theta)\), so Newton-type methods extract curvature without ever assembling the Hessian.

## 3. diff-soup Software Overview

In this section, we introduce the architecture of `diff-soup`, specifically the three primary modules for modeling, simulation, and inference as visually outlined in Figure 3. The modeling module provides the tools for declaring a PDE system, its geometry, and its discretization method through `diff-soup`’s Recipe API to construct a sparse, discrete problem for the time- integrators. The simulation module integrates this system in time using the stiff VSVO algorithms and provides discrete parameter sensitivities. Finally, the inference module solves PDE-constrained optimization problems to learn model parameters from data.

We implement three native optimization algorithms in `diff-soup`: a Newton trust-region method using the exact Hessian or its Gauss-Newton approximation, a Levenberg-Marquardt method, and a limited-memory BFGS method. Additionally, we provide wrappers to the `optax` and `optimistix` libraries for first-order training of embedded deep learning models and for further solvers.

We provide a variety of tools and modules in `diff-soup` for typical inference workflows including data assimilation, batching, and function approximation. Specifically, we provide pre-built tools for projecting image data onto a mesh, refining the mesh, and estimating initial and boundary conditions from image data. For batching, multiple shooting is employed to partition large trajectories into shorter windows that are joined by continuity constraints. This both reduces the computational cost of long trajectory simulations and improves the robustness and conditioning of the optimization problem [93, 25]. In addition, we offer a variety of prebuilt modules for approximating functions and operators that commonly occur in PDEs. Orthogonal polynomials, neural networks, and neural operators are supplied for approximating constitutive relationships, functions, and operators within PDEs. We provide Karhunen-Loève expansions and coordinate networks for approximating spatial fields both classically and using deep learning. Additionally, a variety of differentiable, piecewise interpolants such as constant, linear, and cubic polynomials are offered for time-varying signals.

As discussed in Section 3.2, `diff-soup` employs both data and model parallelism for distributing computation across multiple GPUs. Under data parallelism, subsets of a larger dataset, either distinct experiments or windows for multiple shooting, are distributed across all GPUs, and the losses, gradients, and curvature are then summed across the devices. We specialize this for hierarchical inference problems where the dataset consists of many experiments on distinct domains with multiple episodes per domain. The problem can be distributed into three types of parameters: global parameters shared by all experiments, cluster parameters that are shared by a single domain, and local parameters that are specific to a distinct episode. This allows us to exploit the arrowhead structure of the resulting joint Hessian and employ a block Newton solver that uses a Schur complement over the shared block. Under model parallelism, a single simulation whose sparse factorization outgrows the memory resources of one GPU is factored across<tbc>

several devices.

## 4. Benchmarks

In this section, we benchmark `diff-soup` against widely used scientific computing frameworks for stiff dynamical systems, including the CPU libraries SUNDIALS [31], PETSc [33], `DifferentialEquations.jl` [34], and MATLAB `ode15s` [35], and the GPU-based `JAX` library `diffrax` [49]. We use three problems of increasing complexity: the heat equation, which admits a closed-form solution in both the continuous and the discrete setting, the Brusselator system, which is a model benchmark problem for stiff PDEs [65], and a challenging coupled chemo-mechanical Cahn-Hilliard problem inspired by PFHub benchmark problem 4 [94].

### 4.1. Comparing time integrators with the heat equation

The heat equation on the unit interval with homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries takes the following form:

\(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2},x\in(0,1),t\in(0,T],u(0,t)=u(1,t)=0,u(x,0)=x(1-x),\) (16)

which is discretized with second-order central differences on _N_ interior nodes \(x_i=i\Delta x\) with spacing \(\Delta x=1/(N+1)\) as

\(u'_i=\frac{u_{i-1}-2u_i+u_{i+1}}{\Delta x^2},i=1,\dots,N,u_0=u_{N+1}=0,\) (17)

and integrated to _T_=0.2. Both the continuous problem and the semidiscrete system admit closed-form solutions,

\(u(x,t)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{4\left(1-\left(-1\right)^k\right)}{k^3\pi^3}sin(k\pi x)e^{-k^2\pi^2t},u_i(t)=\sum_{k=1}^N\hat{u}_ksin(k\pi x_i)e^{-\lambda_kt},\lambda_k=\frac{4}{\Delta x^2}sin^2\left(\frac{k\pi\Delta x}{2}\right),\) (18)

where \(\hat{u}_k\) are the discrete sine coefficients of the initial condition and \(\lambda_k\) are the eigenvalues of the negative discrete Laplacian. Figure 4 shows the decay of the solution over the benchmark window.

We note that the eigenvalues of the discrete Laplacian span \(\lambda_1\approx\pi^2\) to \(\lambda_N\approx 4/\Delta x^2\), which causes the stiffness, typically characterized by the ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalues, to grow as _O(N_<sup>2</sup>) [95]. Furthermore, explicit solvers for the heat equation face a CFL limit on the largest stable time step, \(\Delta t<2/\lambda_N\approx\Delta x^2/2\) for the explicit Euler method, due to the coupling of the temporal and spatial discretizations, so the step count grows as _O(N_<sup>2</sup>) regardless of the accuracy requested. As such, it is common to employ implicit time integrators to achieve unconditional stability with respect to the time step. However, implicit time integrators require a linear solve at every step, which creates a computational burden of _O(N_<sup>3</sup>) per step if dense linear solvers are used. By contrast, `diff-soup` uses the adaptive VSVO time integrators described in Section 2.1 with the sparse numerical methods of Section 2.2, which scale quasilinearly in _N_.

## 4.2. Comparing performance with the Brusselator and Cahn-Hilliard problems

To establish the performance of `diff-soup`, we benchmark our solvers against comparable scientific computing libraries that offer stiff time integrators, sparse linear solvers, and sensitivity analysis, namely SUNDIALS, PETSc, `DifferentialEquations.jl`, and `ode15s` in MATLAB. We select the two-dimensional Brusselator and a coupled chemo-mechanical Cahn- Hilliard system as model stiff problems. The Brusselator is a reaction- diffusion model [96] that is a conventional benchmark for stiff integrators [65, 97],

\(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=A+u^2v-(B+1)u+\alpha\nabla^2u,\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=Bu-u^2v+\alpha\nabla^2v,\) (19)

where _u_ and _v_ are the concentrations of the two species, _A_=1 and _B_=3 are the feed and conversion rates, and \(\alpha=1/50\) is the diffusivity. The problem is solved on the unit square for \(t\in[0,10]\), with every wall held at the reaction steady state _u_=1, _v_=3, from the initial condition \(u=1+sin(2\pi x)sin(2\pi y)\),<tbc>

_v_=3. Under these conditions, the system exhibits stiffness from the diffusion term, the nonlinearity, and the oscillatory behavior visible in Figure 6.

To stress-test the solvers, we select the fourth-order Cahn-Hilliard problem coupled to mechanical equilibrium, inspired by the elastic precipitate benchmark of the PFHub phase-field community \[94, 98\], defined as follows:

\(\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot(M\nabla\mu),0=\mu-f'_\mathrm{bulk}(\eta)-\frac{\partial f_\mathrm{el}}{\partial\eta}+\kappa\nabla^2\eta,0=\nabla\cdot\sigma,\sigma=C(\eta):\left(\varepsilon-\varepsilon^0(\eta)\right),\text{(20)}\)

where \(\eta\) is the conserved order parameter, \(\mu\) is its chemical potential, _M_ is the mobility, _f_<sub>bulk</sub> is the bulk free energy, \(\kappa\) is the gradient energy coefficient, \(\varepsilon=\mathrm{sym}(\nabla\mathbf{u})\) is the strain of the displacement **u**, \(\varepsilon^0(\eta)\) is the dilatational misfit strain of the transformed phase, \(C(\eta)\) is the stiffness interpolated between the two phases, and _f_<sub>el</sub> is the elastic energy density. We use an initial condition of two cosine modes with wavelengths near the most unstable wavelength, and integrate the system for \(t\in[0,36]\) s on a \(50\times 50\) nm square domain. This problem is an index-1 DAE with both local differential and algebraic states, and it exhibits significant stiffness due to the fourth-order spatial derivative, the nonlinearity, and the unstable spatial modes shown in Figure 7. ## 4.3. Reduced Precision and Multi-GPU Parallelism

Traditionally, sparse direct solvers have struggled to remain competitive with Newton-Krylov methods for large, three-dimensional problems due to the superlinear growth of their computational cost and memory requirements [76, 73]. However, as discussed in Section 4.2, sparse direct methods have significant robustness advantages over Newton-Krylov methods, which has led us to explore GPU-specific strategies for extending sparse direct methods to three-dimensional problems. Using the three-dimensional Brusselator with<tbc>

For the memory-bound sparse factorization of three-dimensional systems, precision is a significant lever, since many accelerators run Float64 precision at a small fraction of their Float32 precision rate. As seen in Figure 11a, the cost of the Float32 precision solve falls by an order of magnitude at scale, and it prevents the memory overflow of the Float64 precision factor at \(1.8\times 10^6\) degrees of freedom. At matched tolerance, its final state agrees with the Float64 precision solve to within \(4\times 10^{-6}\) in relative _L_<sup>2</sup> norm at every smaller size. Consequently, if the stiffness of the problem tolerates a Float32 precision factor, reduced precision is the most effective acceleration available, especially in three dimensions where the bottleneck is the factorization of the pencil matrix. In reverse mode, the Float32 precision gradient of the Brusselator closure problem on a \(32\times 32\) grid at rtol = 10<sup>-5</sup> agrees with the Float64 precision gradient to a relative _L_<sub>2</sub> error of 10<sup>-3</sup>. Distributing the factorization across devices is a weaker lever, as seen in Figure 11b, roughly halving the cost on two devices and improving only modestly on four.

## 5. Applications to PDE-constrained Optimization

`diff-soup` combines physics modeling, differentiable simulation, and optimization in a single package that serves both classical and deep-learning based inference. In this section, we demonstrate end-to-end workflows implemented entirely in `diff-soup` for two different inference paradigms: a conventional Bayesian inference problem for learning the constitutive relationships of binary phase-separating materials, inspired by Zhao et al. [79] and Cohen et al. [25], and a modern deep learning problem in which a neural field is embedded in a packed bed reactor model and trained to represent its three-dimensional catalyst activity.

### 5.1. Inference with Uncertainty Quantification

First, we demonstrate `diff-soup` on a classic Bayesian inverse problem, in which the constitutive relationships of a phase-separating material are inferred from image data. We reproduce the results of Zhao et al. [79], inferring the composition-dependent tracer diffusivity _D(c_) and the homogeneous chemical potential \(\mu_h(c)\) from a single noisy movie of spinodal decomposition and quantifying the uncertainty by sampling the posterior. The composition _c_ evolves according to the Cahn-Hilliard equation

\(\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot\big(D(c)c\nabla\mu\big),\mu=\mu_h(c)-\kappa\nabla^2c,\) (21)

where \(\mu\) is the chemical potential in units of _k<sub>B</sub>T_ per particle, \(\kappa\) is the gradient energy coefficient, and _D(c_) is the tracer diffusivity, related to the mobility<tbc>

_M(c_)=_cD(c_) by the Einstein relation. We parameterize both functions with orthogonal polynomials,

\(\mu_h(c)=\mathrm{ln}\frac{c}{1-c}+\sum_{k=1}^{12}a_kP_k(c),D(c)=\mathrm{exp}\big(\sum_{k=0}^9b_kP_k(c)\big),\) (22)

where _P<sub>k</sub>_ is the shifted Legendre polynomial of degree _k_ normalized in _L_<sup>2</sup>([0,1]) , the logarithmic term retains the ideal entropy of mixing, the exponential keeps the diffusivity positive, and \(\theta=(a,b)\) collects the coefficients. Following Zhao et al. [79], we assume the coefficients are distributed as

\(a_k,b_k\sim\mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac{s^2}{1+k(k+1)}\big),\) (23)

where the variance decays with the polynomial degree, so that the prior damps oscillations that the data cannot resolve, and the scale _s_ is set by empirical Bayes (Section 7.2). We then solve for the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate

\(\theta^*=\mathrm{argmin}_\theta\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\big\|c(t_i;\theta)-\hat{c}(t_i)\big\|^2-\mathrm{ln}p(\theta),\) (24)

where \(\hat{c}(t_i)\) is the measured frame at time _t<sub>i</sub>_, \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the measurement noise, and \(p(\theta)\) is the prior of Eq. (23). We use multiple shooting, so that each prediction \(c(t_i;\theta)\) is integrated from the previous measured frame \(\hat{c}(t_{i-1})\) rather than from the start of the movie, which keeps each solve short and greatly accelerates the optimization [93]. As in Cohen et al. [25], we treat each measured frame as an exact initial state for its window, so the likelihood of Eq. (24) accounts for the noise in the predicted frame but not in the initial one. We solve Eq. (24) with the Newton trust region algorithm and then sample the posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS) [99] implemented in `blackjax` [53].

## 5.2. Embedded Deep Learning Model

`diff-soup` provides the capability to embed large deep learning models directly into PDE simulations, owing to its foundations in `JAX` and its GPU acceleration. In this example, we demonstrate physics-constrained deep learning at scale by training a neural network through the solution of a three- dimensional packed bed reactor model, in which the network represents the heterogeneous catalyst activity _k_(**x**). The concentration _c_ of the reactant evolves according to the advection-dispersion-reaction equation

\(\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(u_x(y,z)c\big)=\nabla\cdot\big(\mathbf{D}\nabla c\big)-k(\mathbf{x})\frac{c}{K+c},\) (25)

where the reactant enters the bed at the concentration _c_<sub>in</sub>, _u<sub>x</sub>(y,z_) is a fixed velocity profile along the axial coordinate _x_, **D** carries the axial and radial dispersion coefficients, and _K_ is the saturation constant of the Langmuir- Hinshelwood rate law. We generate a synthetic dataset by solving Eq. (25) on a \(96\times 24\times 24\) grid with a known activity field and adding Gaussian noise. The true activity is a log-normal random field multiplied by a poisoning front and a streak of low-activity pellets, which together form a challenging heterogeneous target for the reconstruction. We parameterize the activity field _k_(**x**) with a wavelet-based neural field (WIRE) [100] consisting of \(7.5\times 10^4\) parameters. The final layer is a softplus function to ensure positivity, and we initialize the network to match the uniform nominal activity \(\bar{k}\). Since the neural field depends only on position, it enters the residual as a field and leaves the sparsity pattern of the Jacobian unchanged. We train the neural field by minimizing the mean squared error between the simulated and measured concentrations using the AdamW optimizer [101] with a weight decay of 10<sup>-4</sup> and a peak learning rate of 10<sup>-3</sup> under a linear warmup and cosine decay schedule.

## 6. Conclusion

We have presented `diff-soup`, a software package for GPU-accelerated simulation and inference of large-scale dynamical systems built around the cuDSS sparse direct solver. Accelerating the linear solves of stiff implicit integration on the GPU yields up to \(50\times\) faster simulations and \(80\times\) faster gradients than established CPU libraries. Nonlinear PDEs on structured and unstructured domains are expressed in a general-purpose modeling system, integrated as stiff ODEs and DAEs in `JAX`, and differentiated end to end through the discretize-then-optimize approach. The resulting gradients enable PDE-constrained optimization for both classical and modern inference and learning problems. Our methods were evaluated in a systematic benchmark suite against SUNDIALS, PETSc, `DifferentialEquations.jl`, MATLAB, and `diffrax` on the heat equation, the Brusselator, and a chemo- mechanical Cahn-Hilliard problem, for both forward solves and gradients. We demonstrated these workflows by inferring the constitutive relationships of a phase-separating material with uncertainty quantification and by training a neural field embedded in a three-dimensional packed bed reactor model.

This work has opened up several interesting directions for future study. Specifically, as PDE solvers advance and large-scale physics foundation models emerge, there is a critical need for more rigorous benchmarking of stiff PDEs on both regular and irregular geometries. On the software side, we plan to improve the high-performance computing (HPC) compatibility and acceleration of `diff-soup` with more thorough support for large, distributed simulation and optimization problems. Developing better multi-GPU parallelism strategies for sparse matrix factorization is a promising and important direction of future research. Furthermore, we note the need for support of our algorithms on general accelerator devices and for a modular automatic differentiation library. Finally, we plan to generalize the inference module to adjacent applications of PDE-constrained optimization, such as model pre<tbc>

<tbc>dictive control and design of experiments, and to constrained optimization algorithms like `IPOPT` \[102\].

By modernizing the PDE modeling, simulation, and inference stack, we aim to build an open-source ecosystem for dynamical systems that advances engineering and drives innovation in AI for science.

## 7. Methods

### 7.1. Benchmarking

The benchmarks of Section 4 solve the heat equation, the Brusselator reaction-diffusion system, and the Cahn-Hilliard problem with elasticity. All problems are posed on Cartesian domains, the heat equation discretized by finite differences as in Section 4.1 and the other two by the finite-volume method. The Brusselator adapts the constants of the BRUSS problem of Hairer and Wanner \[65\]. The Cahn-Hilliard problem follows the elastic precipitate benchmark of PFHub \[98\] with a regular-solution bulk free energy, \(f_\mathrm{bulk}=A\left[\eta\mathrm{ln}\eta+(1-\eta)\mathrm{ln}(1-\eta)\right]+\omega\eta(1-\eta)\) with _A_=0.16 and \(\omega=0.40\), a gradient energy coefficient \(\kappa=0.29\) and a mobility _M_=5.0. The misfit strain is a dilatational strain of 0.005, and the cubic stiffness constants are (_C_<sub>1111</sub>_,C_<sub>1122</sub>_,C_<sub>1212</sub>)=(250,150,100) in the matrix and 1.1 times those in the precipitate, both interpolated between the phases by \(h(\eta)=\eta^3(6\eta^2-15\eta+10)\). The initial condition adds two zero-flux cosine modes of index 7 with peak amplitude 0.05 to a uniform composition of 0.5 on a 50 nm square domain. The boundaries are no-flux in \(\eta\) and \(\mu\) and traction free, and three displacement degrees of freedom at two corner cells are pinned to remove the rigid-body modes. In the gradient benchmark, the replaced constitutive relationship in both systems is a pointwise tanh network with two hidden layers of width 128, initialized by LeCun normal initialization \[103\] and fitted with Adam to the term it replaces. Its \(N_\theta\) active weights are drawn from each layer in proportion to its size, the remaining weights are held fixed, and L is the mean squared misfit at eight equally spaced times to target trajectories generated with the weights perturbed by 1%.

Every benchmark runs on nodes of one type in an HPC cluster, with Intel Xeon Platinum 8562Y+ processors and NVIDIA L40S GPUs. In the forward benchmarks, the external comparators run each solve on eight CPU cores, except PETSc, which runs on one, and their hybrid GPU lanes on one L40S and one CPU core. The `diff-soup` lanes of Figures 5, 8, 9 and<tbc>

<tbc>10 run `diff-soup` 1.0.0 with `cuDSS` 1.0.0.35 and `JAX` 0.11.2, with the CPU lanes on KLU over eight cores (one core in Figure 5); Figure 11 and the appendix figures were measured with earlier development versions of the same integrators, and the deposited records provide the benchmark data. The comparators run SUNDIALS 7.8.0, PETSc 3.25.3, Julia 1.12.6 with `OrdinaryDiffEq` 7.8.1 and `SciMLSensitivity` 7.119.13, MATLAB R2025b, and `diffrax` 0.7.0. The full manifest in the companion repository provides the configuration of every benchmark. SUNDIALS [31, 32], PETSc [66, 33] and MATLAB lack a native automatic differentiation library for their integrators, so they are supplied the analytical sparse Jacobian of each problem. `DifferentialEquations.jl` [34] assembles its Jacobian by sparse automatic differentiation with `ForwardDiff.jl` and graph coloring. Reported wall time is the median of the warm calls of one process after one cold call, and we employ a strict wall cap of 1800 s for each benchmark cell to minimize the computational burden of the large benchmark suite. Accuracy is the mean absolute error of the final state against the reference, and for a gradient the relative _L_<sup>2</sup> error against the reference gradient. The Brusselator references are external `CVODE` solves (SciPy `Radau` in one dimension) and the Cahn-Hilliard references are `diff-soup` solves, each at tolerances tightened beyond the plotted range and validated by agreement with a second solve at a neighbouring tolerance. The reference gradients are `diff-soup` reverse- mode gradients at tightened tolerances, validated against a second solve and against central finite differences. Independent SUNDIALS solves reproduce the `diff-soup` references, with `IDA` matching the Cahn-Hilliard reference to \(6\times 10^{-13}\) and the `CVODES` and `IDAS` adjoints matching both reference gradients well below every plotted error.

SUNDIALS integrates the Brusselator with `CVODE` and the Cahn-Hilliard problem with `IDA`, on the KLU [36] and `SuperLU\_MT` [77] direct solvers and on GMRES [39], with and without the ILU(0) preconditioner [74] written for this study. PETSc integrates with `TSBDF` at orders up to five with a lagged Jacobian and preconditioner, and solves the Newton systems with KLU, with GMRES and ILU(0), and with algebraic multigrid. For the Newton-Krylov methods, we tune the Krylov dimension above the library defaults, to 50 on the Brusselator and 60 on the Cahn-Hilliard problem in SUNDIALS and in the ILU(0) lanes of PETSc, and to 100 in the multigrid lanes of PETSc. `DifferentialEquations.jl` integrates with `FBDF` and `QNDF` on KLU and differentiates through `SciMLSensitivity` with a Gauss adjoint in reverse mode and `ForwardDiff` in forward mode. The gradient lanes run Julia on one<tbc>

thread, with 8 BLAS threads for the Cahn-Hilliard problem and 16 for the Brusselator. MATLAB runs `ode15s` \[35\] with the hand-written sparse Jacobian and library defaults otherwise. `diffrax` \[49\] runs `Kvaerno5` and `Tsit5` under its default controller and explicit Euler at the CFL limit in Figure 5. The manifests, the per-lane settings and command lines, the reference tolerances, the step budgets and the record of every cell are in the companion repository named in the data availability statement.

## 7.2. Worked Example 1

The movie of Figure 12 was generated by solving Eq. (21) with the regular- solution laws \(\mu_h(c)=\mathrm{ln}[c/(1-c)]+3\left(1-2c\right)\) and _D(c_)=1-_c_ on the unit square at \(64\times 64\) cells, with \(\kappa=0.002\), no flux and no wetting at the walls, and an initial state of uniform composition 0.5 plus seeded noise. Six frames at geometrically spaced times from _t_=0.1 to 1.0 were corrupted with Gaussian noise at 10% of the standard deviation of the noise-free movie and clipped to \[0.01,0.99\] so that the logarithmic term stays finite. The prior scale _s_ was set by empirical Bayes, scanning the Laplace approximation to the evidence at the fit over six values of _s_ and taking the vertex of the quadratic through the three largest, which gave _s_=1.14. Every window was solved with `JIDA` and `cuDSS` in single precision with forward-mode sensitivities, at rtol = atol =10<sup>-4</sup> in the fit and 10<sup>-6</sup> in the sampler, and the fit took 37 s on one NVIDIA A100, compilation included. The posterior was sampled in four replicates of four chains, each for 200 warmup and 100 sampling transitions, with the chains whitened by the Laplace approximation at the fit, at 1.6 to 1.7 h per replicate. All sixteen chains mixed, with a split \(\hat{R}\) below 1.01 and no divergent transition, and the credible bands of Figure 12 are the pointwise 95% intervals of the two laws over the 1,600 draws. The data generation, the fit and the sampler scripts are in the companion repository named in the data availability statement.

## 7.3. Worked Example 2

The reactor of Figure 13 is a three-dimensional packed bed of dimensions \(4W\times W\times W\), non-dimensionalized by the bed width _W_, the mean superficial speed _U_ and the inlet concentration _c_<sub>in</sub>. The velocity profile _u<sub>x</sub>(y,z_) is the steady solution of the Brinkman equation on the cross-section,

\(\mu_\mathrm{eff}\nabla^2u_x-\frac{\mu}{\kappa_p(y,z)}u_x=\frac{\partial p}{\partial x},u_x=0\text{on the walls},\) (26)

<tbc>with the Kozeny-Carman permeability \(\kappa_p=d_p^2\varepsilon^3/[150(1-\varepsilon)^2]\) and the Vortmeyer-Schuster wall porosity \(\varepsilon(\delta)=\varepsilon_b+(1-\varepsilon_b)e^{-N\delta/d_p}\) at the distance \(\delta\) from the nearest wall, for a particle diameter _d<sub>p</sub>=W/_6, a bulk porosity \(\varepsilon_b=0.4\), _N_=5 and \(\mu_\mathrm{eff}/\mu=8\), scaled to unit mean (Figure 14). The dispersion coefficients follow from particle Péclet numbers of 2 axially and 10 radially, the reactant enters through a Danckwerts flux condition at the inlet and leaves with zero gradient at the outlet, the walls carry no flux, and advection is discretized with central fluxes. The reaction uses \(\bar{k}=0.22U/W\) and _K_=0.05_c_<sub>in</sub>.

The true activity is a log-normal random field with correlation length 0.25_W_ and standard deviation 0.3 in ln_k_, multiplied by a smooth poisoning front that follows the velocity profile and by a cylindrical streak of low- activity pellets at 30% of the surrounding activity. The dataset was generated from an empty bed, saved at every cell at eight times from _t_=1 to 8 and corrupted with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.01_c_<sub>in</sub>. The WIRE network has three hidden layers of width 192 with wavelet parameters \(\omega_0=10\) and _s_<sub>0</sub>=5. The network was trained for 1200 steps on one NVIDIA L40S with the AdamW optimizer \[101\] in `optax` \[52\], every step integrating the model as a single trajectory from _t_=0 with `JNDF` and `cuDSS` in Float32 precision at rtol=10<sup>-5</sup> and atol=10<sup>-6</sup> and using the discrete checkpointed adjoint. Figure B.16: Work-precision (a) and scaling (b) diagrams for the one-dimensional Brusselator for `diff-soup` (solid blue), SUNDIALS (dashed red), PETSc (dashed green), Julia `DifferentialEquations.jl` (dashed purple), and MATLAB (dashed gray), with the marker denoting the particular solver as described in the legend. All benchmarks are run according to the procedure described in Section 7.1. Notably, data points are omitted where the solve did not converge or exceeded the wall cap. Generally, we find that for a one-dimensional problem below the crossover of Figure 5d the fixed overhead of the GPU dominates and the CPU based solvers lead. (a) The work-precision diagram shows the CPU based solvers outperforming `diff-soup`, the fastest of them by over an order of magnitude, with only the multigrid-preconditioned PETSc solver trailing it. (b) The scaling diagram shows `diff-soup` exhibiting a fixed overhead across the ladder, whereas the CPU based solvers exhibit power-law growth.
